content: 1. Administer 4 mg of ondansetron intravenously (IV) or intramuscularly (IM) immediately before anesthesia or after the procedure. Alternatively, administer 16 mg orally (PO) one hour before anesthesia. For patients weighing more than 80 kg, an additional 4 mg IV dose may be required. 2. For total body radiation therapy, administer 8 mg PO 1–2 hours before radiation therapy, repeating the dose daily. 3. For single high-dose fraction radiation therapy to the abdomen, administer 8 mg PO 1–2 hours before radiation therapy. Subsequent doses should be given every 8 hours for 1–2 days after completing therapy. 4. For daily fractions of radiation therapy to the abdomen, administer 8 mg PO 1–2 hours before each session. Subsequent doses should be given every 8 hours after the first dose on each day of therapy. 5. No dose adjustment is necessary for patients with renal impairment. 6. In patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh score ≥ 10), the total daily dose should not exceed 8 mg. This can be divided into 8 mg every 12 hours or 8 mg every 8–12 hours PO for up to 7 days and extended to 5 months if needed. 7. For intermittent short-term IV dosing in adults, administer 4–8 mg. A single 4 mg dose may be used during pregnancy. 8. For spinal opioid therapy prophylaxis, administer 4–8 mg IV 20–30 minutes prior to the procedure. Dosing may be repeated at 12, 24, 36, and 48 hours after spinal opioid administration. 9. For treatment, administer 4–8 mg IV or 4–8 mg PO every 12 hours for up to 3 weeks. Alternatively, administer 12 mg IV daily for 4 days or 10 mg IV every 8 hours as needed. 10. Routine prophylactic use of ondansetron is not recommended by the CDC. However, a single oral dose may be considered for severe gastroenteritis. Dosage is weight-based: 2 mg PO for 8–15 kg, 4 mg PO for >15–30 kg, and 8 mg PO for >30 kg. 11. Ondansetron inhalation powder is used for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in pediatric patients (birth to 16 years) undergoing highly emetogenic chemotherapy. 12. Ondansetron is contraindicated with apomorphine due to reports of profound hypotension and loss of consciousness. Additionally, co-administration may cause additive QT prolongation. 13. Dronedarone increases ondansetron levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and also prolongs the QT interval. This combination is contraindicated. 14. Avoid ondansetron with congenital long QT syndrome. ECG monitoring is recommended when used with medications that prolong the QT interval, in cases of electrolyte abnormalities, congestive heart failure (CHF), or bradyarrhythmias. 15.
